paras: The beating of William Emery was an assault on a jailed man in Holden, Missouri, on the night of about March 9, 1882, when a party of ten citizens took him from the town calaboose and horsewhipped him. The town marshal, H. H. Still, was suspected of leading the party and left town after Emery's neighbors threatened to mob him. Several men were later arrested, and all were acquitted at a hearing before a Holden justice.

Emery, described as a "half-witted young man" who lived north of town, was accused of offering a twelve-year-old girl, Kate Lane, a nickel or some candy if she would kiss him. She refused and reported him, and on Thursday morning he was arrested, charged with "following the girl with evil intent." After a trial he was fined eighteen dollars and costs, twenty-two and a half dollars in all, and, lacking the money, was sent to the calaboose.

That Thursday night a party of ten citizens, "supposed to be under the charge of Marshal H. H. Still," went to the calaboose, took Emery out, and gave him "a severe horsewhipping," pounding him "up terribly." Where the whipping took place is not stated.

On Saturday the vigilance committee of Emery's neighborhood came into Holden and served notice on Still that they would mob him if he did not leave town that night. Still, who claimed to have had no hand in or knowledge of the removal, left on Missouri Pacific train No. 4 and arrived in Sedalia, where he told a Bazoo reporter there was nothing new and then could not be found at the hotels.

Several men were arrested and given a hearing before one of the justices in Holden. All were acquitted, the only evidence against them being that they had been seen on the streets about midnight on the night of the beating. No report names the men arrested or says whether Still was among them.

The only coverage found is in the Sedalia Weekly Bazoo, which printed a special dispatch from Holden on March 14 and a short follow-up on March 28. The first report, headed "SEARCHING FOR STILL," centered on the marshal, saying he fled "not having the sand to face his accusers" and that "Public opinion is high against Still." The follow-up, headed "Not Guilty," said Emery had been "cruelly beaten" but also called him "chastised" and dismissed the affair as "another of Holden's sensations."
Neither article gives the race of Emery, the girl or the men accused of beating him.

bases: A party of ten citizens took Emery out of the Holden calaboose and horsewhipped and beat him; no killing or threat to kill him is reported (A1, A2).

accounts.label: Holden special to the Bazoo
accounts.gist: Ten citizens, supposedly led by Marshal Still, took Emery from the calaboose and horsewhipped him; Emery's neighbors ran Still out of town.

accounts.label: Marshal Still
accounts.gist: Still claimed to have had no hand in or knowledge of taking Emery out of jail, and told a reporter there was nothing new.

accounts.label: Justice's hearing (as reported)
accounts.gist: All the men arrested were acquitted for want of evidence beyond their being seen on the streets about midnight.

framing.detail: The Bazoo called the beating cruel and reported public opinion against Still, but framed the episode as a local sensation about the marshal ('SEARCHING FOR STILL') and closed it as 'another of Holden's sensations', calling the beating a chastisement.
